The Report 


of the 


General Secretary 


of 


The Young Men’s Christian 
Association of Montreal 


oo 
For the Year Ending March 3lst, 1930 


ow 


The 79th Annual Report prescribed by 
the Constitution to present the condition 
and needs of the Association is herewith 
submitted. The accompanying reports of 
the Executive Secretaries of our eight 
Branches and Sir George Williams College 
are of large importance and should be care- 
fully considered with a view to gaining an 
understanding of the manifold activities of 
Grraup W. Brrxs the Association during the year under _J- W- Beatos 


President ip Fee General Secretary 
Montreal Y.M.C.A TEVIEW. Montreal Y.M.C.A. 


The year has been one of intense activity and genuine accomplish- 
ment. It has seen the advancement of the work in many directions and 
has included significant and interesting events in the life of our Movement. 


Finance and Property: 


At the close of our last fiscal year, we 
required an amount of $220,000.00 to 
complete our Building Campaign objective, 
toward which Messrs. J. W. McConnell, 
Gerald W. Birks and T. B. Macaulay had 
promised $80,000.00 conditional on the 
goal being reached. Through the persistent 
efforts of our Finance Committee and 
generous additional gifts and underwritings 

R.C.Horpen by friends, combined with interest earned A. D. Anpznson 

pigharman and the sale of our Papineau Avenue pro- yr hephats 
perty, the amount still required on March 31st was $12,391.60. The 
securing of this latter sum will not enable us to complete our contemplated 


18 


programme as construction costs already definitely ascertained show the 
need of a further sum of $100,000.00 or more notwithstanding a sub- 
stantial saving of approximately $20,000.00 in the construction of the 


Southwestern Branch building. 


An amount of $110,000.00 was provided in our 
Building Campaign for the current operations of the 
Association, and notwithstanding the deficit in our West- 
mount Branch, the amount required from this source 
was $103,000.00, or a saving of $7,000.00 on the Budget 
figures. The consolidated financial statement of the 
Metropolitan Board shows total operating income of 
$386,864.30 and expenditures of $386,784.63, leaving a 
small surplus of $79.67. 


As a nation-wide interest was aroused in the matter, 
we desire to record the judgment rendered during the 


Joun 8, Gipe 
Comptroller 


year by Mr. Justice White of the Superior Court, which maintained 
that in contributing $200,000.00 to the Montreal Joint Hospitals Cam- 
paign in 1927, the Directors of the Bank of Montreal acted within their 
powers as defined in the Federal Act which governs Canadian Banks. 


Membership: 


The membership of the Association on 
March 31st, was 7,088, compared with 
6,641 a year ago, being an increase of 447. 
This constitutes a new record. The in- 
crease is accounted for almost entirely 
through the opening of the Southwestern 
Branch and indicates that our present 
expansion programme is essential if the 
Y.M.C.A. is to keep up with the city’s 


Dent HARRISON W. H. Wurre 
Chairman growth. Retest

These figures, of course, do not include the hundreds of young men 
and boys who join the Association only for the summer months or to 
take advantage of our short term membership, nor do they include the 
thousands of young people who participated in our community pro- 
gramme which is not restricted to membership in the “Y’’, nor the 


14 


constant stream of newcomers to our city who are rendered a large 
number of miscellaneous services without any reference to the fact of 
their membership. 


Foreign Service: 


We are pleased to report an encouraging increase in contributions 
toward the maintenance of Canadian Secretaries in the foreign field, the 
amount being $27,228.87, an increase of $6,651.27 over the previous year.

leadership of our Foreign Work when it acceded to the 
request of Mr. E. I. Taylor, B.A., who for six years had 
been in charge of our International Branch, that he be 
released for service with the boys of China. Reports

Of great importance is the Survey of the Foreign 
Work of the Association throughout the world. Dr. 
E. M. Best, of the United Theological College, and a 
member of our Metropolitan Board, is a member of the 
Survey Staff with special responsibility for Japan, Korea, 
China and the Philippine Islands. It is expected that 
this work will be completed by the end of this year. 


Mr. M. R. Biswas, Secretary of the Boys’ Branch 

of the Y. M. C. A. in Calcutta, returned to India after pr. &. M. Brsr 
spending one year on our staff as Fellowship Secretary. 
His relation to our local work was most helpful and_ letters 
from himself and associates in Calcutta indicate that his contact 
with the Association here was of real value to him and the movement in 
India. He was the third Secretary to whom a fellowship has been 
granted by the Montreal Association. 


Staff Training and Personnel: 


The Montreal Association has 
always emphasized the need of a 
trained secretariat. This is evidenced 
by the increasing number of Univer- 
sity men on our staff, the number 
who attend Summer Schools and 
Training Conferences each year, and 
the emphasis placed on Branch, 
ee oe City-wide and other staff meetings. 


General Secretary : R. E. G. Davis, M.A. 
1874-1913 During the past year we have Secretary 


Cone ee had a staft of thirty-three full time Nat. Personnel Comm. 
and five part time secretaries. Three 

secretaries attended the Training School at Couchiching during the 
summer, one attended the summer session of the School of Education at 
Harvard, and one at Columbia. Staff attendance at conferences and

at Cambridge, Mass.; one took part in the Orientation Week at the

The General Secretary has been the Chairman of the City General 
Secretaries’ Association of North America during the year. 


The staff changes for the year are as follows:— 


Mr. K. E. Norris, B.A., was appointed Registrar and Bursar of 
Sir George Williams College. Mr. Norris graduated from McGill Univer- 
sity a year ago, receiving a special certificate for his high standing in the 
General Arts Course. 


Mr. Sidney Chard resigned his position as Physical Director of the 
Central Branch after several years’ service in the Association. 


16 


Mr. H. C. Patterson, B.P.E., Physical Director at Westmount 
Branch, was transferred to Central Branch to take Mr. Chard’s position. 

Mr. H.R. Ellis resigned his position as Association Physical Director 
at Central Branch on September 1st, and was succeeded by Mr. A. H. 
Reekie, who was transferred from the Boys’ Division at this time. 

Mr. W. H. Spearman was appointed Young Men’s Secretary of 
Central Branch on September 1st, coming from the London, Ontario, 
Association, after several years’ service in that city. 

Mr. E. I. Taylor, B.A., resigned his position as Executive Secretary 
of the International Branch to go to the Foreign Service Division. Mr. 
Taylor and his family have gone to Amoy, China, where Mr. Taylor is 
on the staff of the Association. 

Mr. S. Holtze was transferred from the International Branch to the 
Westmount Branch, replacing Mr. Patterson as Physical Director at the 
latter branch. 

Mr. D. J. F. Scott, B.A., was appointed Executive Secretary of the 
International Branch, succeeding Mr. Taylor. Mr. Scott had for four 
years previously served as part time Secretary. 

Miss L. M. Tufteland (Graduate of McGill School of Physical 
Education) was appointed Associate Secretary of the Southwestern 
Branch, and entered upon her duties there prior to the opening of the 
new building. 

To the staff of the new Notre Dame de Grace Branch have been 
appointed Mr. J. M. Duckworth, M.A., as Executive Secretary, and Mr. 
C. J. McGerrigle, B.A., B.D., as Associate Secretary. Mr. Duckworth 
had a brilliant academic career at McGill University and is completing 
his work at Union Theological Seminary, New York. Mr. McGerrigle 
did his academic work at McGill University and the United Theological 
College. His academic work was of a high grade and he excelled in 
hockey and other athletics. 

During the year the Association has continued to co-operate with 
the Personnel Division of the National Council by giving part-time em- 
ployment and practical training to the Y.M.C.A. students at McGill 
University. Three students were employed by the Boys’ Division of 
Central Branch, one by the Mount Royal Avenue Branch and one by 
Sir George Williams College. 

We deeply regret the loss by death of Mr. Jos. Sykes, who for seven 
years was a faithful and efficient employee of the Central Branch, having 
been elevator operator during that time. The Association policy of 
providing Group Insurance for its employees again proved helpful. 


Kamp Kanawana: 


While attendance was not as high as in 1928 
yet the 1929 aggregate attendance of 1090 boy 
weeks and 347 boys is the second highest in the 
history of the camp. 

The boys came from Montreal, Westmount, 
Outremont, Montreal West, Maisonneuve, Point 
Claire, Verdun, Cote St. Paul, Chateauguay 
Basin, Ormstown, Frelighsburg, Thetford Mines, ae 
Jamaica Plains, New York City, White Plains, aaa a 
Toronto, St. Hilaire and Quebec City. 


17 


The new equipment on Lac Becscies was further advanced by the 
building of a wharf, a new dining pavilion, four new tent floors, and the 
digging of a well. This camp will form a valuable annex to the main 
camp for “‘peak’”’ periods and also for overnight and short term out-trips. 


A new craft shop in Kanawana was built in order to provide addi- 
tional scope to the interest displayed in last year’s experiment in car- 
pentry instruction. Under competent leadership the boys built the 
articles in which they were interested. These interests were also extended 
into camp activities and many improvements in equipment were made 
by the boys themselves. Leadership was also given to the building of 
model aircraft and to basketry. This training in manual skill, and the 
opportunities given the boys for self expression in these models, is one of 
the finest educational advances in our camp program. 

Instruction was also given in rowing, canoeing, first aid, athletics, 
tree lore, boxing, swimming, wrestling, archery, life saving and photo- 
graphy. Tree experts from the Dominion Department of Forestry visited 
the camp and gave valuable leadership. 


Each year we encourage Sunday School classes to 
use the Camp rather than establish separate camps of 
their own. A group from Chateauguay Basin, led by 
Rev. E. T. Prittie, has used our camp now for three 
years with profit to themselves and a real benefit to 
Kanawana. 

Sunday services were held, when weather permitted, 
in the outdoor chapel, and at other times in the Lodge. 
These were periods of real worship and were most helpful 
to the boys. The morning chapel services around the 
flagpole each day helped to maintain the true spirit of 
Christian worship, and the evening devotion by tent groups rounded 
out and interpreted the day's experiences in their relationship to Christian 
living. 

The Fossils Club of Westmount Branch again provided Camp 
Scholarships for fifteen under-privileged boys. A group of business men 
from the Westmount Branch underwrote the expense of twelve boys 
from the Protestant Orphans’ Home and one boy from the School for the 
Blind. 

The season's operation showed a surplus of $201.00, which was 
applied against the capital expenditures of $2,258.00 on the Becscies 
extension and the new craft shop. 


The Camp fee is $8.50 a week, by which it is aimed to keep the 
camp within reach of the average home. 


R. H. Dawson 
Chairman 


Kamp Kanawana is filling an increasingly greater place in the life 
of our city’s boyhood. Camping is one of the finest experiences a boy 
can have, and when this experience is secured under competent Christian 
peste it prepares a boy to take his place as a Canadian Christian 

‘itizen. 


Camp Otoreke: 


The attendance of young men at Camp Otoreke totalled 205 
as compared with 211 in 1928. Organized activities included tennis, 


18 


volley ball, quoits, baseball, aquatics, hiking, 
social evenings, annual regatta, weekly paper 
and Sunday services, all of which contributed 
to the making of a purposeful vacation for this 
camp for young men. The Camp equipment 
was enlarged as follows: Galleries on the pavilion 
were extended and an entirely new kitchen 
erected. A small sleeping cabin was also cons- The Main Cabin 
tructed. 


Metropolitan Boys’ Work: 


The year has been one of fine co-operation in all our Boys’ Work, 
and a real enthusiasm for and a consciousness of a sharing in a work 
that is not only in a local Branch but is City-wide. 


The experiments of having our Father and Son 
Banquets, throughout the city, on one night was again 
tried, and proved decidedly worth while. On November 
25th, five Branches were hosts to a total of 1,235 Fathers 
and Sons, the attendance by Branches being as follows:

Outstanding speakers were secured in each case and the evening 
served to develop a deeper consciousness of fellowship between dad and 
lad. 


Probably the greatest educational values in our city-wide Boys’ 
Work are present in the Montreal Boys’ Hobby Show. Representative 
boys from each Branch formed the Board of Directors and were assisted 
by boys from the Boy Scout Association. For a period of several months 
they met regularly to build up the program of exhibits, securing the 
advertising for the prize booklet, solicited special prizes, enlisted judges, 
and then, when the time for the show came, they received and arranged 
the exhibits and carried out the details of guarding and conducting the 
exhibition. Truly, it was a show for boys by boys. There were 203 
exhibitors with 635 exhibits. 


Inter-branch competition in various activities was very keen and 
through every event the finest sportsmanship and good fellowship existed. 
The annual swimming, basketball and ping-pong championships were 
conducted as usual. In addition, an inter-branch athletic meet for boys 
was held in June. Through the winter, six Branches were represented in 


19 


an inter-branch Juvenile Basketball League for boys under 18 years of 
age. The honors finally went to the Mount Royal Branch. 


In July we had the pleasure of speeding on their way the 23 boys of 
the “Short’’ World Tour. These groups go yearly from the United 
States under the leadership of the National Council, and not only give 
the boys a world travel experience but also broaden their conception of 
world friendships. We were hosts to them before their sailing and also 
welcomed them on their return in September. The experience was, we 
believe, mutually profitable. 


During the year we also welcomed again Mr. Henri Johannot of the 
Boys’ Work Staff of the World’s Committee at Geneva, who was on his 
way to Japan to conduct the first International Camp in Japan. 


At the close of the last school year, the graduating classes of the 
various High Schools of Montreal and district, were invited by the 
S.C.A. of McGill and the Y.M.C.A. to attend a special supper meeting, 
when the prospective students of the University were given helpful 
information regarding ways in which they might make the most of 
college life, especially by establishing right contacts in their freshman 
year. The nucleus of this group of older boys was made up of members 
of our various Hi-Y Clubs in the city. Professor Carleton Stanley was 
the speaker and Dr. I. Gammell the chairman. 


During the year we again co-operated with the newly formed Boy 
Life Council and two of our Secretaries are acting as Secretaries of sub- 
committees of the Council—those on activities and membership. 


The promotion of Kamp Kanawana was in the hands of this com- 
mittee, co-operating with the Camp Committee. This included the very 
successful camp reunion of about 200 old campers at the Southwestern 
Branch. 


We find that throughout the city our boys are more and more assum- 
ing responsibility for the progress in their Branches, and are patcing 
themselves for positions of leadership in the days ahead. 


Religious: 


The Young Men’s Christian Association stands before the world, 
direct and unequivocal as a Christian Association with the advancement 
of the Kingdom of God as the central objective of its many activities. 


It has sought in the year that has gone to guide youth into the way 
of Christ. It has used many methods to accomplish this objective. 
These have included personal interviews, discussion and study groups, 
conferences and forums, fireside sing songs, Sunday afternoon musicales, 
camp-fire talks and devotions, vesper services, resident members’ break- 
fasts, foreign service meetings, observance of the Week of Prayer, as 
well as the manner of conducting all the features of the many sided 
program of character development. 


The 1930 Young Men’s Forum program of the Central Branch was 
again of a most constructive character and was built around the theme:

Metropolitan Physical Education: 


The Physical Education activities of the Association 
have continued to occupy a large and important place in 
the programme of all the Branches. 


The gymnasium classes for all ages of boys from 10 
years up, for young men, and for business men, have 
been well attended. This is the backbone of our work— 
the organized and instructed groups receiving carefully 
planned and progressive training in body-building, health- 
producing and muscular efficiency exercises. The organ- 


: > 1g A J. K. McNurr 
ized classes are the nuclei from which the numerous ete 


games, leagues and sports tournaments are promoted; 
and the men’s classes attract those who have no especial favorite amongst 
indoor sports or who enjoy the all-round programme put on. 


But the Association endeavors to provide the facilities also for those 
who want the specialized sports, and of these basketball has proved the 
most popular. House leagues were conducted by Central, North, Mount 
Royal, Westmount and Railroad; Central alone having 24 men’s teams 
in their Fall, Winter and Spring leagues. The Branches were well repre- 
sented in the various City leagues, with Central and Westmount in the 


ort 
pam | 


Senior; Central (two), Westmount and North in the Intermediate and 
Junior; and the Railroad in the Intermediate. Central Branch partic- 
ularly distinguished themselves this year by winning the Junior Pro- 
vincial Championship and the Junior and Intermediate M.A.A.A. 
Tournaments. This Branch has 150 players in organized basketball. 


Handball and volleyball were prominent games amongst the business 
men and senior members of most of the Branches and tournaments and 
leagues were conducted within and between several Branches. 


Badminton is growing in popularity in those Branches which have 
allotted time and space to it; Westmount, North, Mount Royal and 
Southwestern. The Ladies’ Club at Westmount closed its membership 
at 50 and had a waiting list of 30. 


Gymnastics are popular with certain groups. The Sokol Society of 
International Branch, composed of Czecho-Slovakians, joined Central in 
order to get the use of their gymnasium and met regularly each week 
with over 20 members. The Leaders Corps of Central, Westmount, 
North and Mount Royal gave exhibitions at their own Branches, and 
also combined displays at the Young Men’s Conference in November 
and at the opening of the new Southwestern Building in February. 


Tennis at Westmount, North and Cote St. Paul Branches was 
popular during the summer, with a total of 16 courts. 


Outstanding features in the Branches were as follows: 


1. Central: 


Conducted three Provincial A.A.U. Championships— 
Handball—Seven clubs entered—Won by Central Branch. 
Gymnastics—Four clubs entered—Won by McGill. 
Wrestling—Eight titles out of eight won by Central. The Club 

had 45 members. 


Leaders Corps—Organized a Graduate Leaders Society with 13 
members. Active members numbered fifteen. Gave demonstra- 
tions at Sherbrooke, Shawbridge and Southwestern Branch. 


Medical Examinations given to 536 members by three doctors. 


Boxing Club of 45 members, took part in many invitation meets and 
also City and Provincial Championships. 


2. Westmount: 


. 
Monthly Badminton tournament amongst the Ladies and a closing 
general mixed tournament. 


Weekly classes in gymnasium and swimming for the boys of the Deaf 
and Dumb Institute, School for the Blind and the Protestant 
Orphanage all through the winter, all conducted by members of 
the Senior Leaders. 


22 


3. North: 


Dunlop Road Race in the Fall with 4 teams competing. Dunlop 
shield won outright by North Branch and a new record for the 
course set up. 


A strong fencing club with several open meets. 


4. Verdun: 


Organized and managed a municipal soft ball league for 42 teams 
of boys and girls and a municipal football league of nine teams. 


5. St. Paul: 


Held a monster athletic meet and fair in August, including soccer 
football exhibitions, boxing, softball—230 athletes in the 
athletic meet. Total attendance of spectators, 15,000. Three 
softball leagues for industrial men and boys. 


6. Notre Dame de Grace: 


Cleared their grounds and conducted a free playground for children 
during the summer. 


7. Mount Royal: 


Had great interest and success in basketball with six house leagues 
for all ages. They also won the Juvenile Inter-Y Champion- 
ships (under 18) and the 80-Ib. class Inter-Y Championships. 


The Leaders Corps conducted gymnasium classes in the churches in 
the community. 


Inter-Branch Competitions were conducted as follows: 


Boys’ athletic meet in June for city championship: no prize or 
medals, only certificates; every athlete scored points for his 
Branch. Won by Westmount. 


Tennis and football leagues with 4 and 8 teams respectively compet- 
ing from North, Mount Royal, Central, Westmount and Rail- 
road. 


Swimming meet for boys in March, all Branches being represented. 
Won by Central Branch. 


Basketball tournaments for boys of six weight classes. These were 
Mount Royal—2, Southwestern—2, North—1, Central—1. 


New Features: 


Central and Westmount installed ultra violet lamps in their Health 
Departments, which were quite well patronized.

City-Wide Relationships: 


The leaders of the Association have realized for many years that the 
Y.M.C.A. is one of many agencies at work in the world with the idea of 
establishing a reign of righteousness and to this end has sought to ally 
itself to many organizations working for better social, educational and 
religious conditions in our city. Asa result, much has been accomplished 
in co-operation which would otherwise have been impossible. In some 
cases the part the Y.M.C.A. has played has been a relatively small one; 
at other times it has made a contribution of first importance. 


Among the agencies with which the Association has had the privilege 
of co-operating have been the following:

Sir George Williams College: 


Twelve hundred and six different men and women, boys and girls, 
have been students in the college during the past academic year. This 
represents an increased enrollment over last year of 186. The students 
were registered in the various divisions, as follows:

Of the 1206 students, 391 were sixteen years of age 
or under. The median age was 18.6 years. 


The staff of the College now consists of thirty-seven 
persons. There is an administrative and supervisory 
staff of four, thirty teachers and three stenographers. 


An important appointment during the year was 
that of Mr. K. E. Norris, B.A. (with distinction), McGill, 
as Registrar and Bursar. Mr. Linwood B. Richardson 


was appointed Assistant Registrar. F. O. Srrepper, 
M.A., Px.D., 
The College has always been fortunate in the type Principal 


of men and women which it has been able to attract to 

its teaching staff. The quality of the work done by any educational 
institution is determined by the quality of its teachers. In an evening 
school the teachers must be exceptionally sympathetic and more than 
ordinarily qualified if they are to stimulate the highest type of endeavor 
on the part of the students. 


During the year the following new appointments have been made to 
the teaching staff: 


Marcel Andre, B.A. (Paris), French. 
J. W. Arnott, Shorthand.

W.S. Watson, B.A. (Toronto), English. 


For the first time in its history, the College has offered courses of 
University grade. In response to the insistent demand of a group of 
men and woman, a class was organized, late in the Fall, offering instruc- 
tion in French, English, Mathematics, Latin, History and Physics. 
Thirty students followed the course. Those who are successful in the 
examinations qualify for entrance to the second year of the Arts or Science 
courses of the day University. 


It is very gratifying to announce the following honours which have 
been won by former students of the College and some members of the 
teaching staff: 


Mr. C. H. Cheasley, B.A., who graduated from the Evening High 
School five years ago and then entered McGill University, was awarded 
his Master of Arts degree, with distinction, in the Department of Eco- 
nomics. Mr. Cheasley became re-associated with the College during the 
past session, as instructor in Business Arithmetic and Business English. 


Mr. Alistair Watt, a graduate of our Evening High School four 
years ago, was awarded his Bachelor of Arts degree, with First Class 
Honours and the Lieutenant-Governor’s Silver Medal in History, by 
McGill University. 


Mr. L. J. Crozier, instructor in the Grammar School, was awarded 
his Bachelor of Arts degree (McGill) with First Class Honours in Mathe- 
matics and Physics. 


Mr. J. W. Brunt, B.A. (Queen’s), Supervisor in English in the 
Evening High School, was awarded his Master of Arts degree in English 
by Columbia University. 


Mr. F. S. Hewitt, instructor in the Grammar School, was awarded 
his Bachelor of Arts degree, with First Class Honours, in English and 
Second Class Honours in Philosophy, by McGill University. 


All these instructors are continuing with the College during the next 
session. 


During the year a number of committees have been studying in- 
tensively the various courses of study in the Evening High School, with 
the object of developing materials which are especially adapted to the 
needs of evening school students. Excellent courses of study have been 


27 


produced in the field of English, Mathematics and Science. It has been 
gratifying to receive very favorable comment on these courses from 
several outside educational authorities. 


Central Branch: 


Central Branch, because of its loca- 
tion, has continued to serve thousands of 
young men coming to our city for the first 
time, and who look to the Association as 
the place where they may secure friendly 
advice and assistance. A very great many 
have come to us from Great Britain and 
other European centres, asking for help in 

Lr-Con. Herserr their efforts to get settled. They often 

Eee bring membership cards or letters from Hanoxp C. Cross 

os dane their home Association, and so our service 2ecutive Secretary 
helps to maintain the bond of brotherhood which characterizes our move- 
ment as a world-wide Christian Association. 


The Dormitory accommodation has been greatly overtaxed. Num- 
bers have been turned away who desired to live in the Association. An 
average of 182 men have occupied our dormitories nightly, with a total 
of 3,964 different men for the year. The Council elected by the residents 
has been active and effective, not only in the interests of their group, but 
also in the wider programme of the Branch. 


The Young Men’s Division has shown definite indication of progress 
during the past year. A worthwhile conference was held in November 
when consideration was given to the development of a 
more adequate programme for young men. A Y.M.- 
Y.W. Conference was held at the Isle Aux Cerfs when 
the religious problem of young people was dealt with. 
Several new groups were organized during the year, 
including the Northern Electric, Bell, Bankers and 
Insurance Clubs. A fine series of lectures was conducted 
on the subject of Home Making, and another on Invest- 
ments for Young Men. 


The Library continues to be a popular educational H.-J. Hannarorp 
feature. The Committee has endeavored to secure the Facer ere 
best of the new fiction, biography, science, travel and popular science. 
A monthly meeting of book readers discussed subjects of common interest 
and Dr. S. P. Rose lectured on Modern Biography. A fine assortment of 
Canadian, British and American magazines has been provided for our 
members. 


The Boys’ Division membership was 842. Most of the boys are 
employed full time or after school hours. A worthwhile programme of 
character building activities has been carried out, largely under the 
direction of the Boys’ Cabinet, elected by the boy members themselves. 
Twenty-two organized groups were active, including stamps, mouth 
organ, world service and membership. The hospital choir continued its 
fine work, singing each Sunday morning at the Children’s Memorial 
Hospital. 


28 


The Physical programme served 90,558 individuals. Physical 
examinations were given to 536 members. The new individual Health 
Service, which included ultra-violet, infra-red lamps and massage, proved 
beneficial. The swimming pool was as popular as ever. Free swimming 
campaigns were conducted for schoolboys, employed boys and men. Two 
house basketball leagues were conducted, with 300 players. Provincial 
championships were conducted for the A.A.U. of C. in wrestling, handball 
and gymnastics. Our junior basketball team won the City and also the 
Provincial championships. 


Friendly counsel and guidance to young men and 
boys has always been one of the chief functions of the 
Association. During the year this service has been 
greatly increased in scope and volume. Correspondence 
has been carried on with all parts of the world in this 
connection. Very helpful adjustments have been accom- 
plished in many cases, with the help of ministers, doctors, 
business men and lawyers. The problems dealt with 
included religion, educational, vocational, health, etc. 


: W. J. Hor: 
In the Employment Department a very trying Dv igias.° 


year was experienced, since so many more men applied Secretary 
for help than could be placed in positions. This was 
due to the general business conditions in the city. There 
were 243 calls from firms, 2,726 interviews with men and 
boys, 164 men placed in positions, and 391 were directed 
to places of possible employment. 


There has been continued co-operation with the 
constructive agencies of the community. We have 
endeavored to work with others in the field of social 
reconstruction through supplying a meeting place, 
loaning use of equipment, providing leadership, sharing FRANK SPENCE

in common efforts, etc. Borsa 


The financial report of Central for the year was very satisfactory. 
The Branch was able to earn, through membership fees, dormitory 
rentals, club and business features, 90% of the total cost of operating, 
the balance, 10%, was received from the Joint Fund, and we were able 
to finish the year within our budget allowance.

The Association year begins with the 
end of winter and the opening of the 
summer program. The Association Branch 
at Westmount has served 834 members 
and many non-members in varied ways, all 
with a view of contributing to the growth 
and betterment of those who came to the 
Building. During May, June and July, 104

Regular gymnasium classes have continued and have been well 
lattended. Handball, volleyball and badminton maintained their popu- 
iarity. As always, Westmount had strong teams in various competitions 
in basketball, swimming and hockey. The leaders gave good service. 
They lead floor classes and serve outside groups. Successful ladies’ 
classes were held in the gymnasium. Women also played in the bad- 
minton competitions. 


The Boys’ Work has a large place in the Westmount Branch, 678 
boys being members at different times of the past year. There were 
twelve regular clubs meeting weekly. The Hi-Y club has had a splendid 
year, due to the helpful co-operation of Mr. Mussell and Mr. Parker. 
Inspirational talks and discussions on life problems were undertaken in 
all group activities. The model airplane club and the _ basketry 
club both had successful years. The Hallowe’en social and the Father 
and Son Banquet were the two outstanding social features of the year. 
Twenty-seven boys graduated into the Young Men’s Division. 


There has been much activity in the Young Men’s and Senior 
Divisions. The Fossils Club had the best year of their existence. Their 
annual show was excellent and was repeated at St. Anne’s Military 
Hospital and St. Columba House. The Fossils have done splendid 
charitable service and have made constructive contribution to the boy 
life of Montreal. A new supper club, ‘““The Knights of Swaraj,”’ was 
formed. Westmount young men attended the City Young Men’s Con- 
ference and Westmount Leaders put on an exhibition of physical work 
at that time. 


The Y.M.C.A. is an enterprise which works amongst 31 different 
nationalities the world over. Last year Westmount Branch contributed 
$1,500.00 to the world-wide work of the Young Men’s Christian Associa- 
tion. 


The Women’s Auxiliary has rendered the most faithful and valuable 
assistance of all the many committees. The Board and members are 
extremely happy to remember them with sincere gratitude. 


North Branch: 


In many respects the past year at 
North Branch was a very encouraging one. 
Membership receipts of $4,809.50 were the 
highest in five years. While this is $390.00 
in advance of the previous year, owing to 
close checking® the number of members 
reported is slightly less,—viz: Boys, 302; 
Men, 224; Total, 526. A more active in- 
terest was taken in the Foreign Service 
W, J. Moone enterprise of the Y. M. C. A. Fifty-five Ridin heave 

etc men and a number of boys contributed “7°""" ester 
$552.00. 


A new and successful feature was a series of young men’s supper 
meetings, at which instructive, inspirational addresses were given by 
citizens of standing and ability. These promoted fellowship and practical 
idealism and had an attendance ranging from 40 to 60. 


The aggregate attendance at Physical Department activities was 
substantially greater than the previous year. Members of three Leaders 
Corps received special training and assisted with their respective gym- 
nasium classes. Members of the Track and Field Club competed in 
numerous events locally, and in other cities, and on all occasions carried 
off most of the important prizes. Twelve members received instruction 
in life saving. Two hundred and twenty school boys, not members of 
the “Y”’, registered in a ‘‘Learn to Swim” Campaign and many of them 
succeeded. 


The privileges of the swimming pool have been extended to the 
Mount Royal Branch weekly and scout and church groups on special 
occasions. The Ladies’ Badminton Club has had the use of the gym- 
nasium at hours not required for regular program. 


All activities of the Boys’ Division have provided opportunities for 
character growth. The Secretary and his Committee have endeavored 
to help boys to “‘find themselves” and to guide them into Christian 
living. Program features have been promoted through clubs and hobby 
groups under competent leadership. These have included supper meet- 
ings with addresses, discussions, musical items, debates and Bible study. 
Basketry, rifle shooting, photography, model aircraft, stamp collecting, 
glee singing, hockey, swimming, hikes, “learn something’’ trips, game 
tournaments of checkers, ping pong and billiards, movie shows and 
services of worship have also had a place. The Father and Son Banquet 
in November, at which Canon Allan P. Shatford gave an appropriate 
address, was attended by 320 boys and dads. The annual sleigh drive 
was enjoyed by 112 boys. 388 different boys were members during the 
year, in addition to which hundreds of others were extended courtesies. 


During the year important repairs and improvements were effected, 
and large sections of the building re-decorated and furnishings renewed. 
Much of this work was made possible by a special grant of $1,800.00 from 
the Expansion Fund. 


The generous helpful assistance of the Ladies’ Auxiliary in connec- 
tion with many social events of the year is greatly appreciated. 


The membership of the Board of Management has recently been 
increased from fifteen to twenty-one, of whom four represent the Young 
Men's Division. With these additions and a new alignment of Com- 
mittees, the Board hoped that a more enriching program might be 
provided and that the changing needs of boys and young men might be 
more effectively met.

Southwestern Branch: 


This report of the Southwestern 
Branch covers the eleventh year of 
service in the district of Verdun. It 
includes for the first time activities 
carried on in the new building which 
was opened on February 15th, 1930. 


The contract for the building was let 
April 21st, 1929, and the corner stone 
was laid on October 12th by Mr. Chas. Gin So Moony 
Cuas. Maystne Manning, Chairman of the Board of Executive Secretary 
ena” sas Management of this Branch since its Vereee Pacer ortt 
inception in 1918. 


The week of January 26th, 1930, was set aside for Dedication Week. 
The program was arranged ds follows: 


Sunday—Afternoon tea for the Board of Management and all Com- 
mittees. 

Monday—Luncheon for City Council and City Officials; 
Open House for all School Boys; 
Supper for Boys, Charter Members. 


32 


Tuesday—Luncheon for School Trustees, School Principals and Clergy; 
Open House to Community. 


Wednesday—Open House to Community.

Streams of people visited the building for the full period. And this 
new Branch building of the Montreal Association became recognized as a 
Temple of Youth for the communities of Point St. Charles, Verdun and 
Cote St. Paul, which it was built to serve. 


During the year, twenty-three meetings of the Board of Management 
were held in order to give attention to the details of completing the build- 
ing and providing for its occupation. There were weeks when not a day 
passed without from one to three committee meetings being held. Such 
faithful service on the part of all committees is a striking tribute to the 
faithfulness of those whose labors resulted in a splendid achievement. 


After much consideration it was decided to experiment in this new 
building with a service to the family on the following basis as recorded in 
the Minutes of the Metropolitan Board: 


“That this Board approve the policy of family service 
recommended by the Verdun Board of Management 
following their conferences with representative women of 
their community. The Metropolitan Board concurs in 
their recommendations for a family membership; for the 
employment of a thoroughly trained and experienced 
Women’s Secretary as an associate of the Executive Secre- 
tary with special reference to the program of the Branch; 
that a local committee of representative women be ap- 
pointed to be responsible for the work for women and girls; 
that this committee be given increasing representation on 
the Board as the work develops; that this work be devel- 
oped cautiously and its experimental nature be clearly 
understood by all concerned. 


“While the Metropolitan Board recognizes that no organic 
relation to the women’s organizations of the Churches, to 
the Y.W.C.A., to the Girl Guides, or to other organizations 
carrying on work for women and girls, is feasible at this 
time on account of financial and administrative difficulties, 
they urge the Verdun Board of Management and staff to 
develop the closest possible relations with these organiza- 
tions and in particular with the Young Women’s Christian 
Association, both Local and National.” 


33 


Boys’ Work activities included gymnasium classes, swimming, 
basketball, house leagues, father and son banquets, Hallowe’en concert, 
corn roasts, club socials, tennis tournaments, community softball and 
football leagues. A successful employed boys’ club was organized for 
older boys. The Hi-Y work has continued unabated. A splendid prep. 
hiking club has been formed and met a real need with younger boys. 
A boys’ council has handled the program of the department, interpreting 
the minds of the members. 


Physical classes for women and girls have included instruction from 
Miss L. M. Tufteland, Associate Secretary, in gymnastics, dancing, 
swimming, badminton, basketball and organized games. She has also 
provided valuable club activities. Progress has been marked in achieve- 
ments and health benefits. There have been organized two junior, three 
intermediate and one senior club, enrolling 140. Sewing and handicraft 
clubs are other notable activities. 


Men's work has been handicapped without a Director of Recreation. 
Nevertheless, with the generous help of S. Aitken, the Central Leaders 
Corps, Mr. S. Harrowing, Wm. Bowie, C. J. McGerrigle and F. Sharpe, 
satisfactory progress was made. A regular schedule of events was pro- 
vided. A debating club and a dramatic club got under way and a new 
club for young men—The Argonauts—was formed. The track and field 
club re-organized. Thus the beginnings were made on a regular program 
based on interests. An orchestra was organized including men and 
women. Young people’s dances were held every second week with an 
attendance of 100. Both men and women were members of the Dramatic 
club. 


The Y’s Men’s Club carried on its fifth year of activity. Sing songs 
on the water front drew hundreds of people. The annual children’s auto 
ride was held. The Club continued its service activities for boys as well 
as arranged for educational lectures with McGill University. Dramatics 
and music were also sponsored. 


The new building is very adaptable and the furnishings are unusually 
attractive. A splendid billiard table was the generous gift of Mr. Dent 
Harrison and the radio and victrola were given by Mr. Lewis C. Haskell. 


With the paving of the streets and the filling and levelling of the 
grounds the Association property and building are a distinctive addition 
to the cultural life of the community. 


The membership of the Southwestern Branch reached the high total 
of 857. 


St. Paul Branch: 


The past year marks the tenth year of service in the community. 
The Y.M.C.A. during this time has sought to serve the youth of the 
district irrespective of race or religious affiliation and regardless of whether 
they were members of the Association or not. This service has included 
the organization and promotion of community and athletic leagues; 
helping youth to further equip itself with education; finding positions 
for boys and young men out of employment; co-operating with churches, 
schools and other community organizations. The goal in all the work 
has been to help youth find a better way to live and grow. Much of 


34 


the present varied activity of a recreational nature being carried on by 
other agencies in the community was first promoted by the Y.M.C.A. 


During the past year educational trips have been taken through 
various industries and through pathological departments of McGill 
University. Through the courtesy of the management, the following 
companies were visited: the Daily Star, Bell Telephone Company, 
Walter M. Lowney Company, Purity Ice Cream Company, Chas. Gurd 
Company, Dominion Textile Company, Dent Harrison's, Thos. David- 
son Company, Northern Electric Co., J. M. Aird Company and the 
Peck Rolling Mills. 


The Library which has been replenished this year by the Kiwanis 
Club has now 510 books. Three hundred and seventy-four were used 
by 233 boys. Educational films from the Canadian Pacific Railway 
Company and the Canadian Natoinal Railways and the Associated 
Screen News have proved of great value. 


A physical program has been conducted during the year. With 
assistance from the Westmount and Southwestern Branches, swimming 
programs were carried on. The Association also conducted gym classes, 
hockey, badminton, soccer, softball and wrestling. A monster athletic 
meet and outdoor fair was conducted on the Dominion Textile field, 
230 athletes taking part. 


An interesting social program was conducted throughout the year. 
Tennis, billiards, ping-pong, carpet bowling and socials were well attended. 
The movies provided by the Famous Lasky Company gave entertain- 
ment to 100 boys weekly. 


The membership of this Branch, which is conducted in the 
Gladstone Avenue School Building, stands at 275. 


Of fine memory is the annual Christmas Tree held for the children 
of the district on Christmas Eve. The ‘‘Y’’ distributed over 750 toys 
provided by the Boy Scouts Association.

A story telling period was held every Tuesday afternoon with an

Twelve hundred and sixty-three played basketball in regularly

and fifty swims were taken at the North Branch ‘‘Y’’ by our members.

and sons. The Ladies’ Auxiliary gave the boys numerous feeds and 
movie shows during the year.

$8,843.00 came from the Joint Fund. The expenditure, which included 
last year’s deficit of $93.00, was $10,974.00, leaving a surplus of $232.00. 


International Branch: 


The International Branch has con- 
tinued this year to help the immigrants 
who come to Montreal to find their place 
in the life of the city. At the close of the 
year we have 430 members coming from 
26 different countries. The International 
Branch does much to conserve the good 
qualities which they bring and to help them 
in the many perplexing problems which 
they face in a new country. D. J. Van Bouman, 


R. W. Jounston 


Chairman Executive Secretary 


It is a difficult thing to learn a new 

language under the most favorable conditions; but for an immigrant to 
learn English in Montreal, where so many with whom he works speak 
French, is particularly difficult. Still, a knowledge of English is essential 
to these people both for their own welfare and that of the country. 
Therefore the service rendered by our English classes is very important. 
This year the classes held 735 sessions with a total attendance of 11,888. 
In these classes an attempt is made to impart an understanding of 
Canadian ideals concurrently with the instruction in English. 


While most of the members come in the first instance merely to 
learn English, they soon find that a friendly atmosphere exists among 
these men of so many countries who find themselves sharing the same 
hopes and facing the same difficulties and so they enter into the whole 
life of the Branch. Every Saturday evening from the first of October to 
the first of June concerts and social evenings are arranged. The attend- 
ance at these gatherings averages 125. Frequently the various Consuls 
are present and they give great support and encouragement to the work. 


36 


In this phase of the work especially we enjoy the close co-operation of 
the Y.W.C.A. and the S.C.A. of McGill. 


Every Sunday afternoon from the first of October to the first of 
May a religious service of strictly non-sectarian nature is held, and an 
address is usually given by some business man who has a message of 
cheer and counsel for these new-comers. There is an average attendance 
of sixty young men at these meetings. Refreshments are provided after 
the service and the remainder of the afternoon is spent in a social way. 


One of the new activities of the Branch which is increasing in its 
scope is that of providing concerts for various organizations in the City. 
In this way the New Canadians have an opportunity to show the older 
Canadians the talents which they bring and to make friends among them. 


Fourteen clubs of various national groups, outside of the member- 
ship, made use of the building this year for committee meetings, rehearsals 
for dramatic performances, entertainments and so on. In all 188 such 
meetings were held. This is significant in showing the place that the 
Branch holds in the life of the immigrants in Montreal outside of the 
actual membership. 


No records have been kept of the number of persons helped in such 
matters as finding work, entering hospitals, translation, sending money 
home and so forth, but it would be a very interesting report if it were 
available. 


Notre Dame de Grace, Montreal West and Hampstead: 


The development of this Branch is proceeding sanely. 
Under the advisement of a committee of Association 
friends who were called together informally in May, 
1929, the Secretary, Mr. J. M. C. Duckworth, under- 
took a sociological study of the community to be served. 
This study took in a survey of the churches, schools, 
athletic clubs, playgrounds and general community 
conditions. Interviews were had with the ministers, 
school principals and bank managers, with a view to 
learning the community need and the demand for the 
services of the Young Men’s Christian Association. 
A cordial reception was given the Secretary by all who were consulted, 
and there was a definite feeling on the part of all that the need for the 
Y.M.C.A. in the community was very great. A large number of calls 
were also made upon the subscribers in the district. 


J. M. C. DuckwortH 
M.A. 


Executive Secretary 


Through the courtesy of friends, a topographical survey was made 
of the property now owned by the Association. This was exceedingly 
helpful in laying out preliminary building plans and in setting out the 
playground areas. 


Playground activities were conducted all during the summer months, 
including slides, sand box, baseball, tether tennis and quoits. The 
grounds were in use morning, afternoon and evening. As many as fifty 
children used the grounds in a single day. 


37 


Mr. McGerrigle joined the staff of Notre Dame de Grace in Septem- 
ber and carried on work with the young people in churches and schools 
during the season, whilst Mr. Duckworth finished his B.D. work at 
Union Theological Seminary, New York City. 


Several important meetings of citizens and friends of the Association 
were held during the Winter and Spring, with a view to organizing fora 
district canvass. It was decided to make a joint effort at the time of 
the Spring Campaign to raise money toward the “Building Completion 
Fund.” It was felt that the district to be served had only partially 
contributed to the fund which is necessary to raise a new building. All 
are agreed that to maintain such a unit when it is erected requires the 
friendship and help from a large-sized constituency. 


Progress with New Buildings: 


SOUTHWESTERN BuILDING—During the year 
under review, the first of the three new buildings 
contemplated when our Expansion Campaign 
was launched in 1928, was built, and, on February 
Ist, 1930, was officially opened. The Metro- 
politan Building Committee held 26 meetings 
during the year and their efforts combined with 
the skill of the architects and the excellent work New Verdun-St-Pawi- 
of the contractors have produced a result in the oe Bie Ghanies Brag. 
new Southwestern Building which has won the warm approval of our 
subscribers and members. 


The structure is Georgian in design, with a rustic brick and Indiana 
limestone exterior. The cubic content is 410,000 feet and the building 
contains three social rooms with fire-places; gymnasium, natatorium 
and two shower rooms; auditorium and banquet hall; reading room; 
club rooms for debating societies and religious discussion groups; class 
rooms for informal educational work and boys’ club rooms. 


Sufficient property has been acquired and is being filled and levelled 
so that tennis, football, playground baseball, hockey and skating may 
form part of the Association programme. 


The cost of this project is about $230,000.00 which represents a 
saving on our budget estimates of about $20,000.00. 


DRUMMOND-STANLEY STREET BUILDING—The 
plans for the alterations and additions to the Central 
Branch proved to be a very difficult task because of 
the complexity of hooking up to a twenty-year-old 
structure a new twelve storey addition. They were 
finally completed in March and in April a contract 
was awarded to The Foundation Company of Canada 
at a cost of approximately $865,000.00. The total 
amount of this project, including Architects’ fees and 
furnishings, is approximately $1,000,000.00.

The primary purposes of this second building in — Evening College and 


id é Residence Building 
our expansion program are as follows: 


38 


(a) 


(b) 


(c) 


(d) 


To provide 430 more dormitory rooms for young men who are 
obliged to live away from home, many of them strangers in the city. 


To help finance the current operations of the new Southwestern and 
Notre Dame de Grace buildings where no dormitories are being 
provided. 


To provide class room and science and laboratory space for 1,000 
more students in our evening college. 


To replace the existing boiler room equipment and hot water pipes. 
in the present building, which are worn out after twenty years of 
use. 


To provide three new locker rooms, three new shower rooms, a new 
boxing and wrestling room, three additional handball courts, 
individual health service, new boys’ social rooms, club rooms and 
handicraft class rooms. 


To provide a modern cafeteria with new equipment located on the 
ground floor of the new Stanley Street Building with special rooms 
for club suppers and large banquets. 


To provide for the re-modelling and equipping of the lunch room 
with a soda fountain and other related facilities. 


To re-furnish the lobby and social rooms on the Drummond Street 
side and create again a homelike atmosphere. 


To make available more space for the Metropolitan Offices which 
are to be located on the second floor of the Stanley Street Building. 


One of the most unique features will be the Little Chapel which is 
to be located on the second floor next to the reading room and easy 
of access, yet sufficiently off the busy path so that an individual 
may enter the quietness of this room and feel the spirit of reverence 
and worship. 


The completion of these alterations and extensions will place in the 


hands of the staff, committees and members a powerful tool for the 
moulding of Christian character. 


Notre DAME DE GRACE—The Building Committee and groups of 


Notre Dame de Grace laymen have done a considerable amount of work 
during the year in connection with the preliminary plans for the above 
building, and it is expected that these drawings will be completed at an 
early date with a view to enabling the construction to be completed before 
the end of 1931.

Appreciation: 


There are many factors which combine to make possible a successful 
year’s work in the Y.M.C.A. We are grateful to the many friends who 
have contributed generously of their financial resources; to the workers 
in the Financial and other campaigns; to members of Boards and Com- 
mittees for their frequent counsel, guidance and service; to the many 
volunteers who have served as friendly counsellors of clubs; interviewers; 
speakers; teachers; interpreters; ministers; to the Press; the members 
of the Leaders Corps; the Staff; to the Churches; the Women’s Auxili- 
aries; the Protestant Board of School Comissioners; Railroad and other 
corporations; Parks and Playground Association; the Young Women’s 
Christian Association and many other co-operating agencies. Above all, 
we are in humility grateful to God for His blessing and power. 


Close of Y.M.C.A. War Service: 


Before closing this report we desire to record that on December 5th; 
the Association work in the Rhineland came to an end when the last 
British soldier left Wiesbaden for England. For eleven years the Y.M.- 
C.A. carried on this work, entering Cologne with the British army and 
remaining with it until the last minute of occupation. In the early days 
there were about 100 Y.M.C.A. centres providing for the needs of our 
men and these were gradually reduced until lately, when there were 
only three regular institutions, e.g., Wiesbaden, Bingen and Konegstein. 
In the end, the Y.M.C.A. was the only organization left in the field, even 
the official canteen having closed down before the final evacuation. 
The day before the last contingent of troops left, they paraded in front 
of the Y.M.C.A. and paid an enthusiastic tribute to those whose service 
had brightened their sojourn in a foreign city. Letters were received 


40 


from the G. O. C. expressing his and the army’s warm appreciation of 
the work done by the “Y.’’ Thus the work begun in the first week of 
August, 1914, has ended, and the greatest adventure the Y. M. C.A. ever 
entered upon has been concluded. 


Conclusion: 


When we consider the vast span of the ages and the mighty forces 
that work in nature and history, our year’s work seems insignificant. 
But when we consider that through all the cosmic and historic process 
there runs the purpose of God to bring forth a perfected humanity in 
the likeness of Christ, then the service of our Association, however 
humble, takes on eternal values. We have had the high honour in the 
year just closed of again sharing in God’s purpose for the youth of the 
world, 

“That God, which ever lives and loves, 
One God, one law, one element, 

And one far off, divine event, 

To which the whole creation moves.” 


Alfred Tennyson (‘‘In Memoriam’’) 


Respectfully submitted, 


General Secretary. 


41

FORMS FOR CLAUSES IN WILLS 


The following forms for clauses in Wills may be found to be convenient.by those who 
contemplate making testamentary provision for the Association 


For General Purposes 
I give and bequeath to the YOUNG MEN’S CHRISTIAN 
ASSOCIATION OF MONTREAL the sum of........................dollars 


($ ), to be applied to the uses of said Association. 


For Endowment 
I give and bequeath to the YOUNG MEN’S CHRISTIAN 
ASSOCIATION OF MONTREAL the sum of.......... ...... dollars 
($ ), the same to be added to its regular Endowment Fund 
and the income used for the purpose of said Association. 


For Endowment 


A Residuary Bequest 


All the rest, residue and remainder of my estate, real and 
personal, I give, devise and bequeath to the YOUNG MEN’S 
CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION OF MONTREAL the _ interest 


of this fund to be applied to the uses of said Association. 


Where it is desired that funds be used for a given Branch, it is suggested that 
the following clause be added to any of the suggested forms: preferably for the use of 
GRO. saves anyeasnienkiae kis TONERS 


CONSULT YOUR LAWYER 
As the formalities in making a Will or a Codicil to a Will must 
be most carefully observed, we advise that in such cases one’s 


attorney be consulted.
